chunks.text: Foreword� Food connects us to the land, to the water, and to each other. This cookbook is published as part of the International Year of the Woman Farmer and the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists, two global observances that invite us to look more closely at who grows, raises, catches, processes and prepares the food we eat, and to recognize the contributions of women across agrifood systems. Across every continent, women are custodians of seeds and soils, herders and milk processors, fishers and fish traders, cooks and knowledge-keepers. They manage rangelands, tend crops, harvest from rivers and seas, and pass down techniques refined over generations. Their work underpins food security, nutrition and the resilience of rural communities, yet it remains frequently invisible, undervalued and underpaid. Despite their important contributions to agrifood systems, women are often underrepresented in decision-making. This collection brings together recipes and stories from women and women’s groups working across land, pasture and water systems in every region of the world. Each dish offers a window into a livelihood, a landscape and a set of relationships: between

collection brings together recipes and stories from women and women’s groups working across land, pasture and water systems in every region of the world. Each dish offers a window into a livelihood, a landscape and a set of relationships: between people and animals, people and plants, and people and each other. We hope this cookbook will be read, cooked from and shared. It is offered both as a celebration and as an invitation to continue building food systems shaped by the women who sustain them. Tacko Ndiaye Gender Team Leader at the Rural Transformation and Gender Equality Division Food and Agriculture Organization of the United Nations International Year of the Woman Farmer 7

INTRODUCTION A cross the world’s farms, rangelands, rivers, lakes and coastlines, women are at work. They plant and harvest. They herd and process milk. They fish, farm fish and trade what they catch. They hold knowledge about seed varieties, grazing patterns and seasonal cycles that has been built over generations, often passed from mother to daughter. The International Year of the Woman Farmer and the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists offer an opportunity to recognize this work in its full breadth. Women are central to how agriculture, livestock- keeping and fisheries function, adapt and endure. They manage household food production and market-oriented enterprises. They are often among the first to notice environmental change and to adjust practices in response, frequently while facing unequal access to land, credit, training, markets and decision-making spaces. WOMEN, FOOD SYSTEMS AND THE WORK OF FAO Open the books at FAO and a simple fact comes into view: women are not a side note in agriculture, pastoralism and fisheries. They make up 41 percent of the agricultural workforce worldwide, and in many countries considerably more.

FAO Open the books at FAO and a simple fact comes into view: women are not a side note in agriculture, pastoralism and fisheries. They make up 41 percent of the agricultural workforce worldwide, and in many countries considerably more. They are the hands behind seed selection and crop care, the people who herd animals to water and back, the ones who gut, salt, smoke and sell the catch before it ever reaches a market stall. And yet, across nearly every measure, from land ownership to credit, training, wages and a seat at the table where decisions get made, women face a gap that men in the same roles do not. This gap has a name in development circles: the gender gap in agrifood systems. It is well documented, persistent, and expensive. Closing it would not only change individual lives. It would strengthen food security, improve nutrition outcomes for whole households, and make rural economies more resilient to shocks, whether those shocks come from markets, conflict or a changing climate. 9

© FAO/Luis Tato In 2026, two international observances put this gap, and the people working to close it, at the centre of the global conversation. The International Year of the Woman Farmer, designated by the United Nations General Assembly, spotlights the roles women play across the full span of agrifood value chains, from production and processing to trade and decision-making, and calls for policy reform and investment that turns recognition into measurable change. Alongside it, the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists draws attention to the ecosystems that cover roughly half the Earth’s land surface and to the estimated 1 billion animals herded across them by pastoralist communities present in more than three-quarters of the world’s countries. These two Years are connected by more than a shared calendar. Rangelands and pastoral systems are also food systems, and within them, as on cropland and at the water’s edge, women’s labour and knowledge are foundational, if frequently uncounted. A herder moving animals to fresh grazing, a processor turning milk into cheese that will keep through a dry season, a fish trader who

on cropland and at the water’s edge, women’s labour and knowledge are foundational, if frequently uncounted. A herder moving animals to fresh grazing, a processor turning milk into cheese that will keep through a dry season, a fish trader who knows exactly which buyer will pay fairly for today’s catch: each is contributing to outcomes that matter for the Sustainable Development Goals on hunger, nutrition, gender equality, climate action and life on land and below water. FAO’s role across both observances is to convene, to coordinate with governments, producer organizations and UN partners, and to translate awareness into the kind of structural change that outlasts a single calendar year: secured access to land and resources, stronger extension and financial services, fairer value chains, and a stronger voice for women and pastoralist communities in the policies that affect them. This cookbook sits inside that effort in a small but deliberate way. Every recipe in these pages is traceable to a place, a system and a woman or women’s group whose work sustains it. Read together, they offer a kind of evidence:

sits inside that effort in a small but deliberate way. Every recipe in these pages is traceable to a place, a system and a woman or women’s group whose work sustains it. Read together, they offer a kind of evidence: of skill, of adaptation, of knowledge passed down and put to use every day, in kitchens and on rangelands and at the water’s edge, around the world. ACROSS LAND, PASTURE AND WATER This cookbook is organized around three systems in which women’s work is central. Land brings together stories of women farming staple crops, vegetables, legumes, grains and tree crops, from cassava and fonio to olives and rice, and of the cooperatives, field schools and seed-saving networks through which they organize and share knowledge.

FROM LAND AND WATER Pasture turns to rangelands and pastoral systems, where mobility, seasonality and close relationships with livestock shape both livelihoods and landscapes. Here, women’s roles as herders, milk processors and holders of rangeland knowledge come into view, often in contexts where pastoralism itself is poorly understood by outside observers. Water gathers stories from fisheries and aquaculture, freshwater and marine, inland and coastal, where women fish, farm fish, harvest shellfish and seaweed, process catches, and run the trading networks that move food from water to table. Within each section, recipes and stories sit side by side, reflecting the reality that food, land, water and livelihoods are bound together. WHY A COOKBOOK A cookbook is an unusual format for a publication about agricultural policy and rural livelihoods, so it is worth explaining the choice. The recipe here is a starting point, not the subject. Each dish in this collection is the visible result of work that often goes unseen: the seed selected and saved, the field tended through a season, the herd moved to new grazing, the catch brought in

point, not the subject. Each dish in this collection is the visible result of work that often goes unseen: the seed selected and saved, the field tended through a season, the herd moved to new grazing, the catch brought in and processed, the knowledge of how to combine, ferment or preserve. A bowl of soup or a loaf of bread carries within it months of labour and decision-making that statistics struggle to convey. There is a longer history here worth acknowledging. Cooking has always been more than provision. It is how communities maintain themselves, how knowledge circulates between generations, how people sustain the conditions that make everything else, including collective action, resilience to hardship, and the strength to keep going, possible. The women’s cooperatives, field schools and community groups represented in this book know this. Food is not a byproduct of their work; it is the medium through which knowledge is shared, solidarity practised, and community held together. By tracing each recipe back to the women and women’s groups who grow, raise, catch or gather its ingredients, this cookbook offers

of their work; it is the medium through which knowledge is shared, solidarity practised, and community held together. By tracing each recipe back to the women and women’s groups who grow, raise, catch or gather its ingredients, this cookbook offers a way into stories that might otherwise stay abstract. Food gives readers a shared point of reference across very different contexts, from high-altitude pastures to mangrove coastlines, from rice terraces to reindeer camps. HOW THIS COOKBOOK WAS MADE Each recipe in this collection is paired with a story about a woman, a family or a women’s group, told in their own context and, where possible, in their own words. These stories were gathered through partnerships with local organizations, cooperatives, field schools and community groups, with care taken to represent each contributor’s work and knowledge accurately. The recipes have been tested and adapted for a global kitchen by our cookbook author, a cook, teacher and recipe writer, working closely with the person who shared each recipe – who is not always the woman or group featured in the accompanying story –

and adapted for a global kitchen by our cookbook author, a cook, teacher and recipe writer, working closely with the person who shared each recipe – who is not always the woman or group featured in the accompanying story – to preserve its local ingredients, techniques and traditions, alongside the context needed to understand where it comes from. 11

HOW TO USE THIS BOOK T his cookbook is organized into three sections: Land, Pasture and Water, reflecting the systems introduced above. Within each section, recipes are arranged by country, moving across regions to give a sense of the breadth and diversity of women’s work in agriculture, pastoralism and fisheries worldwide. Each recipe begins with a story: about a woman or a women’s group, their work, and the landscape, livestock or waters they depend on. The recipe itself follows, adapted for cooks anywhere while staying true to its origins. Together, the story and the recipe are meant to be read as one, the dish as an outcome of the work described. At the back of the book, an extended acknowledgements section lists, recipe by recipe, the individuals, cooperatives, projects and partner organizations who contributed to each story and recipe. Readers wishing to learn more, or to support this work directly, are encouraged to start there. 12

FROM LAND AND WATER LAND Start with a seed. Somewhere behind every dish in this section is a decision about which seed to plant, made long before any pot reached the stove. In the highlands of Ecuador, in the cassava fields of the Democratic Republic of the Congo, in olive groves and rice paddies and millet fields across Africa, Asia, the Caucasus and the Pacific, that decision has, for generations, fallen disproportionately to women. Land brings together stories of women growing the staple crops, vegetables, legumes, grains and tree crops that anchor diets and economies: cassava, fonio, teff, rice, beans, moringa, olives, taro, fava beans, herbs and honey. Some of these crops are ancient, cultivated for millennia in forms barely changed. Others are being adapted in real time, as farmers experiment with new varieties, new techniques and new ways of organizing their work to cope with shifting rainfall, degraded soils and volatile markets. What runs through these stories is not only cultivation but stewardship. Many of the women featured here are not working alone. They are members of cooperatives that

organizing their work to cope with shifting rainfall, degraded soils and volatile markets. What runs through these stories is not only cultivation but stewardship. Many of the women featured here are not working alone. They are members of cooperatives that pool land, labour, equipment and risk. They are graduates of farmer field schools, where new techniques are tested on a small plot before being adopted more widely. They are custodians of agrobiodiversity, the often-overlooked variety of crop types and varieties that keeps food systems flexible in the face of pests, disease and climate stress. A single woman’s choice to keep growing an old variety of bean or grain, even as markets push towards a handful of commercial varieties, can matter for food systems far beyond her own field. Access remains the throughline. Across the countries represented in this section, women farmers are less likely than men to hold formal title to the land they work, less likely to access credit on the same terms, and less likely to receive the extension services and training that would let them adopt new

farmers are less likely than men to hold formal title to the land they work, less likely to access credit on the same terms, and less likely to receive the extension services and training that would let them adopt new techniques more quickly. The recipes that follow are a way of seeing past those statistics to the work itself: the planting, the weeding, the harvesting, the saving of seed for next season, and the cooking that turns all of it into a meal. PASTURE Rangelands do not look like farmland, and pastoralism does not look like farming, at least not at first glance. There are no neat rows, no fixed plots, and often there are no fences at all. What there is, instead, is movement: herds following grass and water across seasons, sometimes across borders, in patterns refined over centuries to match the rhythms of land that could not sustain settled agriculture in any other way. Rangelands cover roughly half of the Earth’s land surface, spanning grasslands, savannas, shrublands, deserts, wetlands and high mountain pastures. Pastoralist communities, present in more

to match the rhythms of land that could not sustain settled agriculture in any other way. Rangelands cover roughly half of the Earth’s land surface, spanning grasslands, savannas, shrublands, deserts, wetlands and high mountain pastures. Pastoralist communities, present in more than three-quarters of the world’s countries, manage an estimated 1 billion animals across these landscapes, turning vegetation that humans cannot eat into milk, meat and other foods that sustain millions of people. In doing so, they also maintain ecosystems that store carbon, regulate water and support biodiversity found nowhere else. Within pastoralist communities, women’s roles are the least visible, although they often carry heavier workloads due to high levels of unpaid and invisible work. In many cases, women milk the animals, process that milk into butter, cheese, yoghurt or other products that can be stored, traded or carried on the move. They hold detailed knowledge of which plants are good medicinal plants, how a herd’s condition reflects the health of the land it has grazed, and hold important ethnoveterinary knowledge that they pass on to future generations. 13

The stories in this section, from high mountain pastures to Arctic reindeer-herding communities, from East African rangelands to the Arabian Peninsula, are united less by geography than by this shared relationship between people, animals and land. Mobility, often viewed from outside as a problem to be solved, is in fact the mechanism that makes these systems work: it is how pastoralists avoid overgrazing any single area, how herds find fresh pasture as seasons change, and how communities adapt to a climate that is, in many of these regions, becoming harder to predict. Recognizing women’s role within these systems means recognizing pastoralism itself, on its own terms, as a sophisticated and adaptive way of producing food. WATER Fish does not wait. From the moment it leaves the water, a clock starts running, and what happens in the hours that follow, who cleans it, salts it, smokes it, dries it, carries it to market, sells it, often determines whether a catch becomes income and food or becomes waste. Across the freshwater and marine fisheries represented in this section, that work, the work

cleans it, salts it, smokes it, dries it, carries it to market, sells it, often determines whether a catch becomes income and food or becomes waste. Across the freshwater and marine fisheries represented in this section, that work, the work that happens after the catch, is overwhelmingly done by women. Water gathers stories from inland rivers and lakes, from mangrove coastlines and open ocean, from the Amazon basin to the Pacific islands, from West Africa to East Asia and the Middle East. Some of the women featured here fish themselves, diving or wading for shellfish and seaweed in traditions passed down through generations. Others farm fish in ponds and cages, harvest oysters from mangrove shallows, or run the small-scale processing and trading operations that move fish from boat to plate, often across considerable distances and through informal networks built on trust and reputation. Fish and aquatic foods are a major source of animal protein and essential micronutrients for billions of people, particularly in coastal and riverine communities where alternatives may be limited or costly. Aquaculture now supplies over half of

trust and reputation. Fish and aquatic foods are a major source of animal protein and essential micronutrients for billions of people, particularly in coastal and riverine communities where alternatives may be limited or costly. Aquaculture now supplies over half of the fish consumed globally, easing some pressure on wild stocks alongside continued efforts towards sustainability and equitable access. In both capture fisheries and aquaculture, women’s contributions – as fishers, farmers, processors and traders – are essential to how food moves from water to table, even though women are frequently underrepresented in the data, in fisheries management bodies, and in the policies that govern access to fishing grounds and water resources. Part of the reason women’s work in fisheries remains undercounted is that so much of it happens after the boat comes in. Gutting, salting, smoking, drying, fermenting, packing and selling are not glamorous tasks, and they take place at the margins of what tends to be measured and valued in fisheries statistics. But without this work, a catch does not become food. It is skilled, time-consuming and often physically demanding,

are not glamorous tasks, and they take place at the margins of what tends to be measured and valued in fisheries statistics. But without this work, a catch does not become food. It is skilled, time-consuming and often physically demanding, and it is the step that determines whether a family has income that week, whether a community has protein through a lean season, and whether traditional preservation techniques survive to the next generation. 14

FROM LAND AND WATER The recipes in this section reflect what is done with fish and other aquatic foods once they reach a kitchen: stewed, dried, fermented, smoked, curried, wrapped in leaves, served raw. Behind each dish is a longer chain of decisions and labour, about where to fish, how to process a catch before it spoils, and how to get it to someone willing to buy it. Seeing that chain is part of what this section offers. CONCLUSION The recipes and stories gathered in this collection span continents, climates and culinary traditions, from herb-filled pastries in Azerbaijan to smoked reindeer in Norway, from oyster harvests on the Gambian coast to seaweed curries in the United Republic of Tanzania. What connects them is a simple truth: in every one of these places, women’s knowledge and labour are central to how food reaches the table. Published as part of the International Year of the Woman Farmer and the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists, this cookbook celebrates that contribution across land, where women farm staple crops, manage agrobiodiversity and lead cooperatives;

food reaches the table. Published as part of the International Year of the Woman Farmer and the International Year of Rangelands and Pastoralists, this cookbook celebrates that contribution across land, where women farm staple crops, manage agrobiodiversity and lead cooperatives; across pasture, where women herd livestock, process milk and hold deep knowledge of rangeland systems; and across water, where women fish, farm fish, harvest, process and trade. These two International Years call on governments, organizations and communities to strengthen the conditions under which women farmers and pastoralists work, improving access to land, resources, services, markets and decision-making. The stories in this cookbook put faces, names and places to that call, and are a reminder that the work behind every meal deserves recognition well beyond the kitchen. Readers are invited to cook these recipes, share them, and carry their stories forward. And everyone – governments, institutions, communities and individuals alike – is invited to take up the spirit of these two International Years: to recognize and invest in the women whose work sustains food systems around the world. Azerbaijan� AGE-OLD FARMING TRADITIONS IMPROVE WOMEN’S LIVES Irada Asadova grew up in a small family farm and learned the value of hard work at an early age. After losing her husband, all the responsibilities fell on her shoulders, and she and her daughter worked tirelessly to develop the farm. In Garakhanli village in Tovuz, she brought together a group of local women who cultivated potatoes and grain to form a collective. Using their harvest, they started producing flour and opened a small bakery, creating employment opportunities for several women. The FAO project “Improved food security and rural livelihoods through women´ s economic empowerment” positively transformed the lives of Irada and her cooperative members, both socially and economically. By participating in FAO training programmes, they gained new knowledge and practical experience, including how to use modern irrigation systems. As a result, their work became easier, they saved water, and productivity increased. Today, as the first woman-led cooperative group operating in the region, Irada and her group are expanding their activities, increasing production, and exploring new areas of work. their work became easier, they saved water, and productivity increased. Today, as the first woman-led cooperative group operating in the region, Irada and her group are expanding their activities, increasing production, and exploring new areas of work. Their cooperative cultivates potatoes and grain crops, continuing a farming tradition passed down through generations. Potatoes are grown both for local consumption and for commercial markets, providing one of the main sources of income for agricultural cooperatives such as Irada’s. Fortunately, the cooperative faces no major environmental challenges. The land is fertile, and the group consists of experienced and hardworking women farmers. However, the main challenge is preserving their harvest. During the hot summer months, potatoes and other agricultural products spoil quickly. Limited access to cold storage facilities and suitable warehouse facilities makes it difficult to store the harvest. To overcome this, the cooperative works to bring its products to market as quickly as possible. © Yogendra Banjare/Pexels © Kindel Media/Pexels 18

AZERBAIJAN QUTAB GREEN HERB QUTAB T his recipe was passed down to the women in Irada’s cooperative by their grandmothers. It is prepared by filling the dough with various herbs and greens and cooking it on a saj, a traditional metal cooking pan. The result is a delicious, nutritious and vitamin-rich traditional dish. Qutab can be prepared throughout the year, but the women cook it more often in spring when fresh wild herbs are plentiful. The herbs used in its preparation are high in nutritional value for both children and adults. It is often specially prepared for guests and loved ones visiting from the city. It is both the centrepiece of the local table and a filling, healthy part of meals. In cities and towns, qutab is also a popular street food. In winter, the ingredients are adapted to use those available during the season. The recipe mainly uses greenhouse-grown greens and vegetables such as spinach, coriander, dill, parsley and spring onions. © Taliye Masimova 20

� TWO HARVESTS: HOW CASSAVA FEEDS FAMILIES TWICE Democratic Republic of the Congo In the rolling hills around Mbanza- Ngungu, in Kongo-Central, women are often in their cassava fields before the sun is fully up. As their mothers and grandmothers did before them, they grow cassava (Manihot esculenta) for both harvests: the tubers that fill the family pot, and the tender young leaves they pick by hand, tied into bundles and carried to market, or pounded at home into pondu for the evening meal. In recent years, the work has become less predictable. The rains do not come as they once did, and the soil does not always give back what it used to do. Still, the women continue to adapt, drawing on the knowledge handed down through generations. They stagger their planting, save what they can against a poor season, and read the land in the ways they were taught. When money is needed – for school fees, seeds or the long trip to market – many turn to their village savings and credit associations. There, neighbours pool small

season, and read the land in the ways they were taught. When money is needed – for school fees, seeds or the long trip to market – many turn to their village savings and credit associations. There, neighbours pool small amounts each week and lend to one another when the need arises. It is a community-led system, built on trust and sustained by women’s commitment to supporting one another. For the women of Mbanza-Ngungu, cassava feeds a family twice: once through its roots, and once through its leaves. And each time a mother pounds pondu with her daughter beside her, she passes on something else too: the recipe, the skill and the memory of how to keep going. 22

PONDU/SAKA-SAKA CASSAVA LEAVES AND PALM OIL DEMOCRATIC REPUBLIC OF THE CONGO T his traditional Congolese recipe can be prepared in different ways. It can be served as a daily meal with rice or fufu (semolina), or as part of a meal for special occasions with a meat or fish stew. It is a recipe that has been passed down from generation to generation, from mother to daughter: an integral part of families’ culinary heritage. The names pondu and saka saka are virtually interchangeable. They are also used to describe the bright green-coloured paste of cooked and pounded cassava leaves, which are processed in order to be sold further afield. © Alice Adams Carosi 24

SEED GUARDIAN COMBATS CLIMATE CHANGE �Ecuador Magdalena Laine is a farmer from the Kichwa Indigenous Peoples living in the Ecuadorian Andes. Together with her family, she farms heritage maize varieties at altitudes over 2 500 metres. Their farms are locally known as chakra, a biodiverse agricultural system recognized in 2023 by FAO as a Globally Important Agricultural Heritage System. In addition to nutrition, food security and income, chakra provide Kichwa People with medicine, fuel and fodder. Every Sunday, Magdalena and her daughters rise early to participate in La Pachamama nos alimenta (Mother Earth feeds us), an agroecological market where some 300 Kichwa women gather weekly to sell their produce. At the market, Magdalena and her daughters sell fresh vegetables, grains and eggs, as well as maize flour and bags of native varieties of maize kernels. Right after the harvest, Magdalena and her family store the varieties of maize and select the healthiest, cleanest kernels to be preserved for the next planting season. Her daughter Verónica calls her mother a “seed guardian”: she preserves many native varieties of maize seeds, and

and her family store the varieties of maize and select the healthiest, cleanest kernels to be preserved for the next planting season. Her daughter Verónica calls her mother a “seed guardian”: she preserves many native varieties of maize seeds, and teaches the younger generations the value of these seeds. The plateaus of the Andes offer different altitudes and microclimate variations, and the local chakra hold the secrets to the large array of crops that Kichwa families produce and enjoy. However, extreme weather events related to climate change, like droughts and floods, are now threatening this system, with changing temperatures affecting the crops grown at given altitudes. These changes may also erode the knowledge that Kichwa women pass down to new generations, for instance when a certain crop needs to be planted. With the financial and technical support of FAO, farmers’ organizations like the Unión de Organizaciones Campesinas Indígenas 26

FROM LAND AND WATER • PART 1 de Cotacachi (UNORCAC) are implementing several initiatives to strengthen the climate resilience of Kichwa communities, for example diversifying food production through the use and exchange of native seeds. Indeed, saving heritage grains is part of a strategy to transform the agrifood sector with a vision of inclusive rural development. Verónica is confident that the ancestral knowledge passed to her by her mother will help her – and future generations – overcome the challenges of climate change. In this effort, women are key. According to Verónica, “women are the ones with the initiative… When I have my own family, I have to sow as my mother did, the same way she taught me. Everything she taught me will stay with me, and I should continue this wisdom.” According to Verónica, “women are the ones with the initiative… When I have my own family, I will have to sow as my mother did, the same way she taught me. SOPA DE CHUCHUCA TRADITIONAL ANDEAN CHUCHUCA SOUP ECUADOR T his traditional recipe is a true reflection of the chakra system. The protagonist of this dish is chuchuca, a partially matured maize that undergoes an ancestral preservation technique of sun- drying and milling. This recipe, shared by Magdalena Laine with the support of the UNORCAC Women’s Committee, perfectly illustrates the nutritional wisdom of Andean women farmers. The dish combines the complex carbohydrates of preserved maize with the plant-based protein of fresh beans and the rich collagen of meat broth, creating a deeply nourishing and comforting meal that has fed generations. © FAO Ecuador 28

THE FAVA BEAN: A STAPLE FOR EVERY TABLE Egypt� Fava beans (Vicia faba) are a traditional and well-established crop in many Egyptian provinces, and represent one of Egypt’s most important legume staples. Aswan and Upper Egypt have been cultivating fava for generations. Like in other regions, fava are tied closely to local food culture. Fava beans are mainly consumed as food, especially in common traditional forms such as ful medames, ta‘ameya (Egyptian green falafel) and other home-cooked dishes. Many farming households traditionally keep part of the harvest for their own consumption throughout the year. Fava also enable Egyptian women to turn food preparation into a livelihood: female entrepreneurship – highlighted as a regional priority – has seen many turn their ta’ameya making skills into micro-businesses, selling sandwiches in village markets or catering stalls. Beyond food use, farmers traditionally value fava beans for their role in improving soil fertility and reducing the need for fertilizer in cereal-based rotations, which helps maintain soil productivity in the hot and dry conditions of Upper Egypt. Teff is highly valued for its exceptional nutritional profile: it is naturally gluten-free and is rich in fibre, iron, calcium and essential amino acids, making it one of the most nutrient-dense grains in the world. The name teff comes from the Amharic word for "lost", because its small size historically made it hard to handle. Teff (Eragrostis teff) can grow well in moisture-stressed and waterlogged conditions, better than other cereals. It is mainly cultivated in the central and northwest highland areas: the Central Ethiopia Regional State and the South Ethiopia Regional State; Amhara; and Tigray, in that order. Made primarily from teff flour, injera is a soft, spongy flatbread that serves as both plate and utensil in Ethiopian cuisine. For Christabel Kwasi, a 29-year-old farmer and mother of three, fonio (Digitaria exilis) is both a crop and a source of confidence. Seeing her children enjoy the rich, nourishing porridge she prepares from the grain she grows is a reminder of what her work makes possible: healthy food on the table, and the satisfaction of knowing that her harvest helps sustain her family. Fonio is an ancient indigenous West African cereal, and is traditionally cultivated by women farmers. In the Chereponi region of Northern Ghana, it is a staple food for farmers like Christabel. Once boiled, fonio resembles couscous. It can be consumed as such, or made into porridge. It can even be turned into flour for baking. It is a versatile crop that generations have relied on, for both food and livelihoods. “I realized that my family likes fonio, and they depend on fonio more than any other food crop,” says Christabel. “Fonio is the type [of crop where] if you don’t even have money to buy chemicals [fertilizers], you can still farm it, feed on it.” Until as

and they depend on fonio more than any other food crop,” says Christabel. “Fonio is the type [of crop where] if you don’t even have money to buy chemicals [fertilizers], you can still farm it, feed on it.” Until as recently as a year ago, Christabel thought she had to wait for periods of rainfall and rely on arduous traditional methods of cultivation to grow fonio, which often left her family with little to no harvest during the dry season. However, a project recently implemented by FAO, in collaboration with Chef Fatmata Binta, renowned for bringing African gastronomy to the global scene, is giving Christabel and other farmers the knowledge needed to grow fonio year- round. Together with Ghana’s Ministry of Food and Agriculture, the project aims to support women fonio producers in Ghana to enhance their cultivation skills and boost productivity and income. Through training sessions on better production and post-harvest techniques, women fonio producers learned to increase their yields and properly store their grains to prevent food loss. In Ghana, also the manual methods of post- harvest handling and processing – mostly undertaken by women – are exhausting processes impacting their yields. � MORINGA: A PLANT VALUED FOR ITS LEAVES, PODS AND SEEDS Niger Moringa (Moringa oleifera) is a cash crop in the Niger, consumed daily as a leafy vegetable in rural and urban areas. The main production areas are in Maradi, Tillabéry, Dosso, Tahoua and Niamey. An important crop for nutritional security, it was introduced to the Niger in the early twentieth century. Moringa leaves are rich in protein and calories. Women mainly ensure the retail sale of moringa in markets. They are practically absent from wholesale trade but also from cultivation, because they often cannot own land (due to customary laws), especially to cultivate a plant that can remain unproductive for more than 15 years and is similar to a perennial crop. However, particularly in the Maradi region, part of the moringa is processed by women. They buy fresh leaves from producers and pre-cook and dry them, before selling the processed product to traders who collect, repackage and resell the dried leaves. As with many foods, proper preparation is necessary to avoid losing too many nutrients, especially vitamins destroyed by the heat of cooking. Also, the leaves should be consumed quickly after harvesting and cooked for only a short time. It is important to conserve and use the liquid in which they are cooked, which also has nutritional value. Moringa leaves are an economical source of protein, vitamins and minerals. Consumed as a national dish, several moringa-based recipes are produced during traditional ceremonies. Sixty percent of Nigeriens consume moringa daily, and demand is influenced by daily habits and festive periods. Recently, local hotel and restaurant chains have started incorporating moringa into their menus. 53

DAMBOU WITH MORINGA NIGER D ambou is an emblematic dish from the Niger, traditionally made with moringa and millet semolina, although these days rice semolina is more commonly used. In the Niger, when we talk about dambou, we refer to the Djerma, an ethnic group concentrated in the Dosso and Tillabéry region, where this recipe is very typical. Dambou has become a national dish, consumed daily either for breakfast or more frequently for lunch. However, it is also commonly found at wedding and baptism ceremonies. It often accompanies a meat dish such as gabagaba, a recipe based on pounded chicken and peanuts. © Alice Adams Carosi 55
